claim.why_it_matters: A heading at the wrong level (or none) misplaces the clause in the outline that page_workunit, citation and section lookups read, so the clause is attributed to the wrong parent or not found as a section.
claim.note: Heading at the wrong level: the transcription's convention is one '#' per numbering component (7. is '#', 7.1 '##', 6.4.1 '###', 6.4.2.1 '####', 6.4.2.1.1 '#####'); should be '#####'.

verdict.reasoning: Printed page IV-38 (PDF p.184) shows the heading '6.4.2.2.1 Definition of Compiler Directing Statement', a five-component number. The heading text in specs/ANSI_COBOL_1985.md line 7685 matches exactly, but it is '####'. Within the same section the transcription puts the five-component sibling 6.4.2.1.1 at '#####' (line 7631) and 6.4.2 at '###', 6.4.2.1 at '####', so 6.4.2.2.1 sits one level too high relative to its equal-depth sibling. That is an outline defect, not only visual formatting: the heading level is what places the clause in the tree. Caveat on the claim's wording: the one-'#'-per-component convention is not file-wide (17 five-component headings are at '####' and 14 at '#####'), and this heading is one level below its parent 6.4.2.2, which is itself misleveled at '###' (claim p184-2). The root of the shift is p184-2; this heading must be lowered together with it.
verdict.corrected_description: Heading 6.4.2.2.1 (text correct) is '####' while its equal-depth sibling 6.4.2.1.1 is '#####'; it inherits a one-level shift from its parent 6.4.2.2 at '###' (p184-2). Fix by setting 6.4.2.2 to '####' and 6.4.2.2.1 to '#####'. The 'one # per component' convention holds within 6.4.2 but is not uniform across the file.
